Patient Information

Exercise for Parkinson's Disease

A comprehensive home programme — big movements, fast movements, hard aerobic work and balance training — built on the principles behind PD Warrior and LSVT BIG.

Exercise is not an optional extra in Parkinson's disease. It is the only intervention with any credible evidence of altering the course of the condition rather than merely masking the symptoms, and it improves almost every aspect of it — walking, balance, mood, sleep, constipation, and probably thinking.

But the type of exercise matters more here than in almost any other condition. Gentle, comfortable, repetitive exercise is worth very little. What the brain responds to is movement that is big, fast, hard, complicated and meaningful to you — which is exactly what the PD Warrior and LSVT BIG approaches are built on.

The central problem this programme is designed to solve

Parkinson's does not only slow your movements — it recalibrates your sense of how big a movement needs to be. A step that feels normal from the inside is visibly small from the outside. That is why you cannot simply be told to 'take bigger steps': you have to be trained to produce movements that feel excessive, because those are the ones that look and function normally.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.
Parkinson's-specific safety — read before starting
  • Exercise during your 'on' time, when your medication is working — usually 45 to 90 minutes after a dose. Never do balance work, stepping drills or intervals while 'off': freezing is more common and lasts longer then, and the fall risk is materially higher.
  • Watch your blood pressure on standing. This is the commonest reason home exercise goes wrong in Parkinson's. Drink a large glass of water fifteen minutes before you start, rise in stages, and start seated if you are prone to it.
  • Get cardiac clearance before high-intensity work if you have known heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, a rhythm problem or valve disease.
  • Ballistic and power exercises need something to hold. Fast movements plus impaired balance is the highest-risk combination on this page. Bench, wall or chair, always.
  • If you freeze, do not fight it. Pushing forward against stuck feet — or being pulled by a helper — is a classic mechanism of falls. Stop first, then use a strategy.
  • Do not exercise when drowsy. Dopamine agonists can cause sudden-onset sleepiness.
  • Keep overhead arm movements below shoulder height if your shoulder is painful. Frozen shoulder is common in Parkinson's and is often one of its earliest symptoms.
  • Mind the heat. Parkinson's impairs sweating and temperature regulation — exercise indoors in the cool part of the day in summer, and stop earlier than you think you need to.
  • If you have had a fall recently, or your Parkinson's is advanced, this should not be a solo home programme. The falls-prevention trials found the benefit concentrated in mild to moderate disease, and no reduction in falls in more advanced disease. Ask me to arrange supervision.
Before you start — making this safe to do alone
  • Always have something solid to grab. A kitchen bench, a heavy table, a wall on each side, or the back of a chair wedged against a wall. Not a wheeled chair, not a towel rail.
  • Choose the right floor. Bare, level, non-slip. Move rugs and cords out of the way. Do not do balance work on a rug edge or a wet bathroom floor.
  • Wear shoes or bare feet, not socks. Well-fitting shoes with a firm heel counter and a thin sole let you feel the floor.
  • If you have fallen in the last six months, or you feel unsafe standing still with your feet together, do not start alone. Do these first with a family member present, or ask me to arrange a physiotherapist.
  • Carry your phone, or wear a personal alarm, if you live alone.
  • Stop and contact your doctor if an exercise causes chest pain, sudden severe dizziness, a new weakness, or a fall.

Why 'big, fast and difficult' is the prescription

The principles below come from the neuroplasticity research that underpins PD Warrior and LSVT BIG. They explain why the exercises on this page look the way they do.

📏 Amplitude

Train movements that are deliberately too big. Your internal calibration is set too small, so 'too big' is what produces normal.

⚡ Power and speed

Parkinson's slows the starting and the speed of movement more than it weakens muscle. Explosive, ballistic movement trains precisely the deficit.

🔥 High effort

Comfortable exercise produces little. The trials that changed outcomes worked people hard — up to 80–85% of maximum heart rate.

🔁 Frequency

Little and often, and permanently. The benefits fade within weeks of stopping, in every trial that has looked.

🧩 Complexity

Add thinking, changes of direction, changes of rhythm. A complicated task engages far more of the brain than a repetitive one.

❤️ Salience and enjoyment

The brain rewires around movements that matter to you. This is not sentimentality — it is why an exercise you enjoy outperforms one you endure, and why group classes work.

Part 1 — Think BIG

Start every session here. Five minutes, and it sets the calibration for everything that follows.

Think BIG warm-up

5 minutes at the start of every session
Amplitude training

Parkinson's shrinks movement without telling you it is doing so — your 'normal' feels normal from the inside while looking small from the outside. Every session starts by deliberately over-doing the size of movement.

  1. Stand tall behind a firm chair, hands resting on it if needed.
  2. Big reaches: reach one arm as high above your head as you can, stretching your fingers to the ceiling and letting your chest open and your eyes follow your hand. Alternate arms, 10 each.
  3. Big side reaches: reach out and across to the opposite side, letting your trunk rotate. 10 each side.
  4. Big steps on the spot: march with exaggerated knee lift and an exaggerated arm swing, as if in a military parade. 20 steps.
  5. Big shoulder rolls and chest opening: roll your shoulders back 10 times, pulling your shoulder blades together and standing as tall as you can.
  6. Everything should feel about twice as big as it needs to be. That feeling of 'too much' is the point — it usually looks about right.
Make it harderAdd speed once the size is reliable. Then do the same movements without hand support, then with your eyes closed for a few repetitions.
Make it easierDo it seated in a firm chair — the amplitude principle works just as well sitting down.
SafetyChair or bench in reach for every exercise. Do this during your 'on' time, when your medication is working.
Why it worksHigh-amplitude training is the core of both LSVT BIG and the Australian PD Warrior programme, and it works by recalibrating the internal sense of how big a movement needs to be.

Posture reset against the wall

5 × 20 seconds, twice a day
Anti-stoop

Counteracts the forward stoop, which shortens your stride, tips your balance forwards and makes freezing more likely.

  1. Stand with your back against a wall, heels a few centimetres out from it.
  2. Press your bottom, your upper back and, if you can, the back of your head against the wall. If your head does not reach, do not force it — get as close as is comfortable and let it improve over weeks.
  3. Pull your shoulder blades back towards the wall and open your chest.
  4. Hold for 20 seconds, breathing normally, then step away and try to keep that height as you walk a few steps.
  5. Repeat five times.
Make it harderAdd slow arm slides up the wall (wall angels). Hold the position for longer.
Make it easierSit in a firm chair against the wall and do the same thing.
SafetyDo not force your head back if your neck is stiff or painful.
Why it worksPostural exercise is a standard component of Parkinson's physiotherapy; a stooped posture measurably shortens stride length and shifts the centre of mass towards the toes.

Big writing and other carry-over

5 minutes daily, plus reminders through the day
Amplitude off the mat

Amplitude training is useless if it stays in the exercise session. The point is to make BIG the way you move all day.

  1. Take lined paper and write the alphabet, deliberately filling the full height between two lines for every letter.
  2. Then write a sentence about your day, keeping every letter equally large — most people's writing shrinks by the end of a line, and watching for that is the exercise.
  3. Through the day, pick three ordinary movements and do them deliberately big: standing up from a chair, stepping over the door threshold, and reaching into a cupboard.
  4. Speak deliberately loudly at the same time — the voice shrinks along with the movement, and both respond to the same 'go bigger' strategy.
Make it harderAdd a daily 'big' task — sweeping, gardening, throwing a ball — that demands large movements naturally.
Make it easierJust the alphabet, once a day.
SafetyNone.
Why it worksLSVT BIG and LSVT LOUD share a single principle: recalibrating the internal sense of effort so that normal-sized movement and normal-volume speech stop feeling excessive. If your voice is becoming quiet, ask me about a speech pathology referral.

Part 2 — Ballistic and power work

The PD Warrior element: fast, explosive, deliberately effortful. Three days a week.

Ballistic punching

30 seconds of work, 30 seconds of rest × 6 rounds
PD Warrior style — power

Parkinson's slows the initiation and speed of movement more than it weakens muscle. Fast, explosive movement trains exactly what the disease takes away, and it is the reason boxing-style classes have become so popular in Parkinson's.

  1. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in a stable split stance, beside a bench or with a wall behind you.
  2. Bring both fists up in front of your chest.
  3. Punch one arm forward as fast and as far as you can — full extension, with a sharp snap, letting your trunk rotate with the punch — and pull it back just as fast.
  4. Alternate arms, punching as explosively as you can manage for 30 seconds.
  5. Rest 30 seconds. Repeat for six rounds.
  6. Then do the same with upward punches and with cross-body punches, so you cover different directions.
Make it harderPunch to a target (a cushion held up, or spots marked on a wall). Add stepping forward and back with the punches. Add a count-down out loud to make it a dual task.
Make it easierDo it seated, or with one hand on the bench and one punching.
SafetyNever punch anything solid — air, or a soft cushion held loosely. If you have shoulder problems, reduce the range. If you are unsteady, sit down for this one; explosive movement plus poor balance is how people fall.
Why it worksPower and speed training addresses bradykinesia directly, and high effort, complexity and salience are core neuroplasticity principles. Be aware of the honest state of the evidence for the boxing classes this resembles: two systematic reviews published in 2025, covering thirteen studies, found no significant effect of boxing programmes on mobility, balance, motor symptoms or fitness — the enthusiasm for them currently runs ahead of the trial data. The case for training power and amplitude is much stronger than the case for any particular branded class.

Explosive sit-to-stand

8 fast repetitions × 3 sets, 3 days a week
Power + function

Getting out of a chair is the movement most affected by Parkinson's and the one that most often ends in a fall. Trained fast, it also builds the leg power that fades earliest.

  1. Firm chair, back against a wall. Feet flat, heels drawn back under your knees.
  2. Lean forward — nose over toes — and count '3, 2, 1, UP'.
  3. Stand up as fast as you can, driving through your heels and coming all the way to full height with a strong squeeze of the buttocks.
  4. Lower back down slowly, over 3 seconds, with control.
  5. Eight repetitions, then rest a minute. Three sets.
Make it harderFold your arms across your chest. Then add a reach for the ceiling at the top of each stand. Then use a lower chair.
Make it easierPush off your thighs; use a higher seat; drop the speed and simply do controlled repetitions.
SafetyFast standing can drop your blood pressure. If you feel light-headed on standing, stand up more slowly, pause holding the chair, and tell me — orthostatic drops are common in Parkinson's and are treatable.
Why it worksThe countdown before the movement is itself a treatment: an external cue like this bypasses the faulty internal 'go' signal, and is the same principle used for freezing of gait.

Progressive resistance training

2 sessions a week, 2–3 sets of 8–12 repetitions
Strongest single trial result

Builds the muscle strength that Parkinson's and age erode together, and it has produced some of the largest and most durable improvements in motor scores of any exercise trial in this disease.

  1. Pick five or six movements covering the whole body: sit-to-stand or a supported squat, step-ups, heel raises, a row or a pull with a resistance band anchored in a door, a chest press or wall push-up, and a shoulder press only if your shoulders are comfortable.
  2. Choose a resistance where the last two repetitions of a set of ten feel genuinely hard but your form does not break down.
  3. Two to three sets of 8 to 12 repetitions of each, resting a minute or two between sets.
  4. Lift with intent — push fast on the effort, and lower slowly over three seconds.
  5. Add a little weight or another repetition when a set stops feeling hard. Progression is what makes it 'progressive', and it is the part people skip.
  6. Two sessions a week is enough. This is the studied dose.
Make it harderMore weight, then more sets. Household weights work: tins, water bottles, a loaded backpack. Resistance bands are cheap and travel well.
Make it easierBody weight alone, fewer repetitions, and seated versions of the upper-body movements.
SafetyBreathe out on the effort — do not hold your breath. Keep overhead pressing light or leave it out if your shoulder is painful, which is common in Parkinson's. If you have osteoporosis, avoid loaded forward bending.
Why it worksIn a two-year trial, twice-weekly progressive resistance training improved off-medication motor scores by 7.3 points more than a stretching and balance comparator — one of the largest and longest-sustained results in the Parkinson's exercise literature.

Fast feet

20 seconds × 5, with rests
Speed drill

Trains rapid, repeated stepping — the ability to get a foot down quickly when you are pushed or trip.

  1. Stand facing the kitchen bench with both hands on it.
  2. Step rapidly on the spot, small quick steps, as fast as you can manage cleanly, for 20 seconds.
  3. Rest for 40 seconds.
  4. Repeat five times.
  5. Speed matters more than height here — this is the one exercise where small is fine.
Make it harderFingertip support; then tapping the feet on and off a low step; then adding a count-down out loud while you do it.
Make it easierSlow marching on the spot with both hands supported.
SafetyBoth hands on a solid surface until you are confident. Stop if you feel your feet 'sticking' to the floor and use the freezing strategies below.
Why it worksRapid stepping trains the same system as the protective step reaction, and speed-focused training addresses bradykinesia in a way that strength training alone does not.

Big steps in four directions

10 steps in each of 4 directions, daily
Amplitude + balance

Trains the long, deliberate step that shuffling steals, in every direction you actually need to move.

  1. Stand beside a bench with one hand resting on it.
  2. Forward: take one deliberately long step forward, landing heel first, then step back to the start. Ten times with each leg.
  3. Backward: take one long step back, landing on the ball of the foot, then return. Ten each leg. Check behind you first.
  4. Sideways: take one wide step out to the side and return. Ten each way.
  5. Diagonal: step long and diagonally forwards, then back. Ten each way.
  6. Every step should be bigger than feels natural, with a firm heel strike you can hear.
Make it harderReduce hand support; add speed; call out the direction to yourself before each step; have someone call directions at random.
Make it easierSmaller steps with both hands on the bench, and keep to forwards and sideways only.
SafetyClear floor, no rugs, bench within reach. Backward stepping is the one most likely to cause a fall — keep a hand on the bench for it.
Why it worksStep training in multiple directions targets the protective stepping response, which is impaired in Parkinson's and is the last defence against a fall.

Part 3 — Aerobic exercise

The part with the most interesting evidence of all. Four days a week.

High-intensity aerobic exercise

30 minutes, 4 days a week, at 80–85% of maximum heart rate
Possible disease-modifying effect

This is the exercise with the most interesting evidence in Parkinson's — the possibility that it does not merely treat symptoms but slows progression.

  1. Choose something you can do vigorously and safely: a stationary bike is the safest choice, then a treadmill with rails, then brisk outdoor walking, then swimming.
  2. Warm up for 5 minutes at an easy pace.
  3. Work for 30 minutes at an intensity where you are breathing hard and can speak only a few words at a time. If you use a heart-rate monitor, aim for 80–85% of your maximum (roughly 220 minus your age, though this is only an estimate).
  4. If 30 continuous minutes is too much, break it into 5-minute hard blocks with 2 minutes easy between them, and build up.
  5. Cool down for 5 minutes.
  6. Four days a week is the studied dose.
Make it harderIncrease duration first, then intensity. Add hills or resistance on the bike.
Make it easierStart at a moderate intensity (60–65% of maximum heart rate) — that is the comparison arm in the trials, and it is far better than nothing.
SafetyAsk me before starting high-intensity exercise — and cardiac clearance is not optional if you have known heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, a significant rhythm problem or valve disease. Drink a large glass of water fifteen minutes beforehand, and start seated if you get light-headed on standing. Exercise in the cool part of the day: Parkinson's impairs sweating and temperature control, which matters in a Sydney summer. A stationary bike removes almost all the falls risk and is the right choice if your balance is impaired.
Why it worksIn the SPARX2 trial (JAMA Neurology, 2018), 128 people with newly diagnosed, untreated Parkinson's exercised on a treadmill four days a week for six months. High intensity — 80–85% of maximum heart rate — proved safe and achievable, and that group's motor scores were essentially unchanged over six months while the usual-care group's worsened; moderate intensity did not show the same effect. A separate Dutch trial (Park-in-Shape) used a home exercise bike with a game-based app and found an improvement of around four points in off-medication motor scores over six months. The larger SPARX3 trial was designed to test whether any of this genuinely slows the disease.

Part 4 — Balance

Because most of what causes harm in Parkinson's, causes it by way of a fall.

Weight shifts and reaching

10 shifts in each direction, daily
Starting point

Teaches you where your limits of balance actually are, and how to move to the edge of them and come back without panicking.

  1. Stand at the bench, feet hip-width apart, hands lightly resting on it.
  2. Keeping your body straight like a tall mast, sway slowly forwards over your toes, then back over your heels. Go only as far as you can come back from.
  3. Do ten of those, then sway slowly side to side, taking your weight over one foot then the other, ten times.
  4. Then reach one hand slowly out to the side and across your body, following your hand with your eyes, and return.
  5. Finish by reaching down towards a spot on the floor beside your foot and back up.
Make it harderReduce hand support; increase how far you reach; reach to place and pick up an object on a low stool.
Make it easierDo it seated on a firm chair first, or with both hands on the bench and very small movements.
SafetySmall ranges first. The point is control, not distance.
Why it worksReaching while standing is one of the functional balance tasks named in the 2022 World Falls Guidelines, and it directly rehearses the movements that cause household falls.

Tandem and semi-tandem standing

3 × 30 seconds each foot in front, daily
Foundation

The static version of tandem walking — the safest way to start if walking heel-to-toe is still too much.

  1. Stand beside a kitchen bench with one hand resting on it.
  2. Put one foot half a step in front of the other, heel beside the opposite big toe (semi-tandem).
  3. Hold for 30 seconds, breathing normally, eyes ahead.
  4. Swap which foot is in front and repeat.
  5. When 30 seconds is comfortable, move the front foot fully in front (true tandem) so heel touches toe.
Make it harderOne fingertip on the bench, then no hands, then eyes closed with a hand hovering over the bench — eyes closed doubles the difficulty and is where the real gains are.
Make it easierFeet together, both hands on the bench, 30 seconds.
SafetyStand facing into the corner of a bench, not out into the room, so there is something to catch on either side. Do this during 'on' time only.
Why it worksFeet-together, semi-tandem and tandem stance are the standard progression used in the Otago programme and in nearly every trial that reduced falls.

Single-leg standing

Build to 15–30 seconds each leg, with hand support, daily
Otago exercise

Almost every step you take is a moment of standing on one leg. This trains the hip and ankle muscles that stop you toppling sideways.

  1. Stand at the bench with both hands on it.
  2. Shift your weight fully onto one leg and lift the other foot a few centimetres off the floor — just enough to clear it.
  3. Keep the standing knee soft, hips level, and look at a fixed point ahead.
  4. Hold as long as you can steadily, up to 30 seconds, then swap.
  5. Do two rounds on each leg.
Make it harderTwo fingers on the bench → one finger → hands hovering just above it. Then add slow head turns, or stand on a firm cushion.
Make it easierKeep the toes of the lifted foot resting lightly on the floor (a 'kickstand'), taking almost no weight.
SafetyAlways within arm's reach of support. Do not test yourself in the middle of the room to 'see how long you can last'.
Why it worksSingle-leg stance time is one of the balance tests used to decide who needs a falls intervention. Being unable to hold it for 10 seconds is a marker worth telling me about — it has been linked to higher mortality and to injurious falls, though it is a warning light rather than a target in itself.

Tandem walking (heel-to-toe), corridor only

10 steps × 3, once a day
Core balance drill

Trains the side-to-side balance control that keeps you upright when you turn, step around something, or are jostled.

  1. Do this in a corridor narrow enough that you can touch both walls with your elbows out, or beside a kitchen bench. Never in the middle of a room.
  2. Stand at one end with your fingertips lightly brushing one wall.
  3. Place one foot directly in front of the other so the heel of the front foot touches the toes of the back foot, as if walking a tightrope.
  4. Take ten slow heel-to-toe steps, looking ahead at a point on the wall rather than at your feet.
  5. Turn around carefully — wide, slow steps, not a quick pivot — and walk back.
  6. Rest, then repeat twice more.
Make it harderFingertips off the wall; then adding a big deliberate arm swing; then walking heel-to-toe to a beat you count out loud.
Make it easierWalk with one whole hand on the wall, and use a semi-tandem step (front heel beside the back toes, not in front of them) until that feels steady.
SafetyNever in an open room, never on a rug, never in socks. If you find yourself repeatedly grabbing the wall, the drill is too hard — go back a stage.
Why it worksNarrowing your base of support is the most efficient way to challenge balance, and challenging balance is what makes falls prevention work. In the Cochrane review of 108 trials, exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% overall — but programmes that genuinely challenged balance and totalled three or more hours a week reduced falls by around 40%. Comfortable, seated, low-dose programmes did not.

Heel raises (calf strength)

10–15 repetitions × 2 sets, 3 days a week
Otago exercise

The calf is the engine of push-off in walking and the first muscle that catches you when you sway forwards.

  1. Stand at the bench, feet hip-width apart, hands resting on it for balance only.
  2. Rise up onto the balls of both feet as high as you can.
  3. Pause for a second at the top — most people cheat this part.
  4. Lower slowly, taking about 3 seconds, until your heels touch the floor.
  5. Repeat 10 to 15 times.
Make it harderFingertip support only. Then single-leg heel raises (holding the bench), building to 10 each side. Then do them with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step so the heel drops below the step — only with a solid rail.
Make it easierSmaller range, both hands on the bench, and do them seated first if standing is unsteady.
SafetyIf you get calf cramps, reduce the number and stretch afterwards. Stop if you get sudden calf pain and swelling — that needs assessment.
Why it worksCalf strength and ankle power decline steeply with age and correlate closely with walking speed, which itself predicts falls, hospitalisation and independence.

Step-ups on the bottom stair

10 step-ups each leg, 2 sets, 3 days a week
Power + confidence

Rebuilds the leg power you need for stairs, kerbs and buses, and rehearses the exact task people become frightened of.

  1. Use the bottom step of a staircase with a solid handrail, or a sturdy step block.
  2. Hold the rail. Place one whole foot on the step.
  3. Push down through that heel to lift yourself up — try to let the leg on the step do the work rather than pushing off the floor with the back foot.
  4. Step back down slowly, leading with the same leg, and touch down quietly.
  5. Do 10 with that leg, then swap.
Make it harderLight fingertip contact on the rail; then a slower 3-second lowering; then a higher step (only with a rail).
Make it easierA single low step or a thick book taped down; or start by simply stepping up and down onto a doorway threshold.
SafetyHandrail in hand for every repetition until you are certain. Shoes on.
Why it worksStair negotiation demands more strength than walking and is where a lot of serious falls occur, so it is worth training deliberately rather than avoiding.

Part 5 — Complexity, freezing and real life

The bridge between the exercises and the day.

Doing two things at once, on purpose

5 minutes, most days
Real-world training

In Parkinson's, walking stops being automatic and starts requiring attention. That is why people freeze in doorways while talking, or fall while carrying a cup. Practising it deliberately, in a safe place, is how you get some of that automaticity back.

  1. Walk up and down a clear corridor at your normal pace.
  2. As you walk, add a thinking task: count backwards from 100 in threes, name as many animals as you can beginning with 'B', or recite the months of the year backwards.
  3. Then add a carrying task: walk while carrying a tray with an empty cup on it.
  4. If you notice your steps shrinking or your voice fading, stop, reset your posture, take a big breath, and start again deliberately BIG.
  5. Five minutes is plenty.
Make it harderHarder mental tasks; carrying something less stable; adding a turn at each end.
Make it easierDo the thinking task standing still first, then while marching on the spot with a hand on the bench.
SafetyCorridor only, with a clear floor, during 'on' time. Do not practise dual tasking on stairs. If you have had a fall in the last month, or you have been told you have significant memory or attention problems, do this with someone present rather than alone.
Why it worksDual-task training improves walking under dual-task conditions. The blanket old advice to 'never do two things at once' is out of date: a randomised trial of 121 people with Parkinson's found dual-task training improved dual-task walking speed without increasing falls. The caution that remains is specific — significant cognitive impairment, or a recent fall, means this should be supervised rather than practised alone.

Getting out of a freeze

Rehearse weekly so it is automatic when you need it
Cueing strategies

Freezing — feet glued to the floor, usually at doorways, on turns, in crowds, or when hurrying — does not respond to trying harder. It responds to changing the task.

  1. Stop. Do not fight it, and do not let anyone pull you. Struggling forwards while your feet are stuck is exactly how people fall.
  2. Stand tall and shift your weight from side to side a few times to break the deadlock.
  3. Give yourself an external cue — this is the key. Count out loud '1, 2, 3, GO'. March to a rhythm. Hum a marching tune. Some people carry a metronome app or a music playlist at about 100–120 beats per minute.
  4. Give yourself a visual target: step over a line on the floor, over the handle of an upturned walking stick, or over your own foot placed in front of you. Aim for a specific floor tile.
  5. Make the first step deliberately huge and heel-first rather than shuffling forwards.
  6. For turns: never pivot on the spot. Walk a wide arc, like a clock hand, taking marching steps around it.
Make it harderPractise with a family member so they know to cue you rather than pull you. Identify your own personal triggers — doorways, the bathroom, the phone ringing — and rehearse the strategy in exactly those places.
Make it easierStart with counting out loud as the single strategy and add others later.
SafetyFreezing is a major cause of falls. If it is new or worsening, tell me — the timing relative to your medication doses matters, and freezing that occurs only when the medication is wearing off is often treatable by adjusting it.
Why it worksExternal cueing works by bypassing the damaged internal timing system in the basal ganglia and routing movement through intact pathways, and it is a standard recommendation of the European Physiotherapy Guideline for Parkinson's Disease. Two honest points: cueing is a permanent strategy, not a course — in the RESCUE trial the gains had largely faded six weeks after the training stopped — and one cue does not fit all. Some people respond dramatically to visual cues such as a line on the floor or a laser, others to rhythm and counting. Try several and keep the ones that work for you.

A week that covers all of it

This is more than most people start with. Build up to it over a couple of months — begin with Parts 1 and 2, three days a week.

DaySessionRoughly
MondayThink BIG warm-up · ballistic and power work · balance40 min
TuesdayAerobic — bike or brisk walk, hard40 min
WednesdayThink BIG warm-up · balance · dual-task corridor work30 min
ThursdayAerobic — bike or brisk walk, hard40 min
FridayThink BIG warm-up · ballistic and power work · balance40 min
SaturdayAerobic, or a class — boxing, dance, Tai Chi, PD Warrior group45–60 min
SundayAerobic or an easy walk · big writing · posture resets30 min

Big writing, posture resets and the freezing strategies are practised daily, in among everything else, rather than as a separate session.

Doing this with other people

Home exercise works. Supervised and group exercise works better, and people keep doing it for longer.

🥊 PD Warrior

An Australian programme built around exactly the principles on this page, delivered by accredited physiotherapists and exercise physiologists, with classes across the country and an online option. To be straightforward with you: the principles it applies are well supported, while the branded package itself rests on a small uncontrolled pilot rather than a randomised trial. That is not a reason to avoid it — supervision, progression and company are worth a great deal — but do not choose it over another good programme on the assumption that it has been proven superior.

📣 LSVT BIG (and LSVT LOUD)

An intensive amplitude-training protocol — sixteen one-hour sessions, four a week for four weeks, with a certified therapist, plus daily homework and carry-over tasks. It clearly outperformed unsupervised generic home exercise in a German randomised trial. Worth knowing: a much shorter and cheaper amplitude protocol produced very similar motor gains, which suggests it is the 'think and move BIG' principle doing the work rather than the sixteen-session package. LSVT LOUD does the same job for a quiet voice.

🤸 Group classes

Dance for Parkinson's, Tai Chi, hydrotherapy and boxing-style classes all have a following, and all deliver the two things a sheet cannot: supervision and company. On the evidence, tango and dance have produced good results in small trials, while two 2025 reviews of Parkinson's boxing programmes found no significant effect on mobility, balance or motor symptoms. Choose the one you will keep attending — that matters more than the label.

🇦🇺 Parkinson's NSW and equivalents

State Parkinson's organisations run support groups, exercise classes and a nurse helpline, and can tell you what exists near you. Your GP can also arrange subsidised allied health sessions — see below.

Questions people ask me

"Will exercise slow my Parkinson's down?"

Possibly — and this is the most interesting question in the field. High-intensity treadmill exercise at 80–85% of maximum heart rate, four days a week, was tested in newly diagnosed, untreated patients in the SPARX2 trial: it proved safe, and the motor scores of the high-intensity group were essentially unchanged over six months while the control group's worsened. That is a promising signal, not proof, and the larger SPARX3 trial was designed to answer it properly.

What is beyond argument is that exercise improves how you function now — across the trials it reduces falls by around a quarter, and two years of twice-weekly resistance training improved off-medication motor scores by more than seven points. And that the benefit fades within weeks of stopping.

"Should I exercise before or after my tablets?"

After. Aim for the window when your medication is clearly working, typically 45 to 90 minutes after a dose. If you are consistently 'off' when you want to exercise, that is a reason to review the timing of your doses with me rather than to exercise 'off'.

"I get very light-headed when I stand up quickly."

Common in Parkinson's, and treatable. Rise in stages — sit on the edge, count to ten, stand holding something, count to ten again. Increase your salt and fluid intake unless you have been told not to, and tell me: some of the medications used for Parkinson's contribute, and there are treatments for the blood pressure drop itself.

"Is it safe to do fast, explosive movements at my age?"

With something solid to hold, and during 'on' time — yes, and it is one of the most useful things you can do. Power fades faster than strength with both age and Parkinson's, and it is power that gets you out of a chair and stops you falling. If your balance is significantly impaired, do the ballistic work seated: you keep most of the benefit and lose the risk.

"Will exercise stop me falling?"

It reduces falls in Parkinson's by around a quarter, which is worthwhile — but with an important caveat: the benefit in the trials was concentrated in people with mild to moderate disease. In more advanced Parkinson's, and particularly where there is significant cognitive impairment, exercise programmes have not reduced falls, and the answer shifts towards supervision, home modification, and managing the specific causes.

If you are falling, tell me. It changes what I would advise you to do on your own.

"I freeze in doorways. Is that laziness or fear?"

Neither. It is a failure of the brain's internal 'go' signal, and it responds to external cues rather than to effort — counting out loud, a beat, a line to step over, a deliberately huge first step. Practise the strategies in Part 5 when you are not frozen, so they are automatic when you are. And tell me when it happens, because freezing that appears as a dose wears off is often treatable by adjusting the medication.

"My handwriting has shrunk and my voice has gone quiet. Is that the same problem?"

Yes — the same loss of amplitude, in the hand and in the voice. Both respond to the same 'go bigger' training. Practise big writing daily, and ask me about a speech pathology referral for the voice; LSVT LOUD is very effective for it.

"How long before I notice a difference?"

Most people notice something within four to six weeks, and the trials generally ran for eight to twelve weeks or longer. The honest catch is that the gains disappear if you stop, so the aim is a routine you can sustain for years, not a course you complete.

"Will I use up my dopamine if I exercise hard?"

No. There is no reserve to deplete, and the evidence points firmly the other way — higher intensity is associated with better outcomes. Fatigue is real and worth pacing around, but it is not a sign that you are spending something you cannot replace.

"I'm on good medication now. Does exercise still matter?"

Yes, and the trials make this unusually clear: the improvements from resistance training and from dance were measured off medication, which means the exercise is doing something the tablets are not. They work on different things, and you want both.

If you do fall: the plan you make in advance

Long lies on the floor cause far more harm than the fall itself. Rehearse this before you need it.

1

Do not rush to get up

Lie still for a moment. Check whether anything hurts badly, and whether you can move both arms and both legs. If you suspect a broken bone, or you hit your head, or you are on blood thinners, call for help and stay where you are.

2

Roll, crawl, kneel, rise

Roll onto your side, then onto your hands and knees. Crawl to a solid chair or a bed. Put both hands on the seat, bring your strongest leg up so that foot is flat on the floor, then push up through that leg and both arms and turn to sit.

3

If you cannot get up

Get to a warm place if you can — drag a blanket or cushion down. Keep moving your arms and legs to protect your skin and circulation. Bang on a wall or floor. This is exactly what a personal alarm pendant is for, and why it must be worn rather than left on the bedside table.

4

Tell me about it

Every fall is worth reporting, even one you were not hurt by. A fall is the single strongest predictor of the next fall, and most causes are treatable — blood pressure medication, vision, inner ear, sensation in the feet, or simple loss of leg strength.

Being honest about the evidence: teaching people to get up off the floor is widely recommended on the strength of the harm caused by long lies — about half of uninjured people who fall cannot get up unaided, and pressure injury, dehydration, muscle breakdown, hypothermia and pneumonia all follow from lying there. The trials that have tested floor-rise training are small and have not shown a clear change in the ability to rise. Rehearse it anyway: the cost is five minutes and the plan itself is worth having.
Hurt is not the same as harm

Muscles that have worked will ache. As a rule of thumb, discomfort up to about 4 or 5 out of 10 during and after exercise is acceptable, provided it settles back to your normal level within 24 hours and is not getting worse week on week. Sharp, sudden or one-sided pain is a reason to stop.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting extra help in Australia

You do not have to do this alone, and supervised programmes work better than unsupervised ones for people at higher risk.

🩺 Your GP can subsidise allied health

Since 1 July 2025, GP Management Plans and Team Care Arrangements have been replaced by the GP Chronic Condition Management Plan. With one in place, you can access up to five Medicare-rebated allied health services per calendar year — shared across all disciplines, so five physiotherapy sessions means none left for anything else (ten services for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients). Referral is now by an ordinary letter rather than a special form. Ask your GP whether you are eligible.

🏃 Physiotherapist or exercise physiologist

A physiotherapist is the right choice for a specific problem — a painful neck, an unsteady gait, vestibular rehabilitation. An accredited exercise physiologist is the right choice for building and supervising a long-term conditioning programme. Both can be seen privately without a referral.

👥 Community falls programmes

NSW Health and many local councils run group strength-and-balance programmes such as Stepping On. Group programmes add the two things a home sheet cannot: supervision and company. Ask your GP or your local council, or search Active and Healthy NSW.

🏠 My Aged Care and NDIS

If you are over 65 and finding daily tasks harder, a My Aged Care assessment can fund home exercise support, home modifications such as rails, and an occupational therapy home-safety visit. Under 65 with a permanent disability, the same supports may be available through the NDIS.

Tell me if
  • You have had a fall, or you are having near-falls or freezing episodes that are new or worsening.
  • You feel light-headed on standing, or you have blacked out.
  • Your symptoms fluctuate markedly through the day — this usually means the medication timing needs adjusting.
  • You are getting involuntary writhing or fidgety movements (dyskinesia), especially if they interfere with exercise.
  • Your voice is becoming quiet, or you are coughing or choking on food or drink.
  • Exercise consistently makes you feel unwell, breathless out of proportion, or brings on chest pain.
  • Your mood has dropped, or you have stopped doing things you used to enjoy — depression and apathy are part of Parkinson's, and both are treatable.
